uksc/2022/25.rationale: This is the leading and directly on-point authority on the question. uksc/2022/34.rationale: This Supreme Court judgment is directly on point. It restates and applies the Sequana / West Mercia / Kinsela line of authority to identify precisely when directors must take account of creditors' interests: the duty arises on the onset of insolvency (when the company is on the verge of, or enters, insolvent liquidation), becoming paramount where insolvency is hopeless, and requiring creditors' interests to be given appropriate weight and balanced against shareholders' interests before liquidation becomes inevitable (s.214 engaged). uksc/2016/11.rationale:
This is the leading modern UK Supreme Court authority on exactly the question asked: vicarious liability of an employer for an employee (a shop assistant) who assaulted a customer, decided in March 2016 and therefore before 2017. The Supreme Court held the employer liable, rejecting the Court of Appeal's "close connection" gloss on Lister v Hesley Hall and explaining that the Lister test is already sound and needs no reform. It is directly on point and is the pivotal case any lawyer researching employer liability for employee assaults on customers would cite, and it also reviews the leading line of authorities (Warren v Henlys, Lloyd v Grace, Smith & Co, Lister, Catholic Child Welfare Society, Bazley v Curry) which is exactly what the question calls for.

On the highlights: all three quoted passages come from Lord Toulson's analysis of the connection between the employee's duties and the assault and state the basis on which the employer was held liable — the abuse of the position entrusted to him in connection with the business of serving customers, and the unauthorised mode of performing assigned duties. It is a leading Court of Appeal authority on vicarious liability for an employee's tort (including deliberate/assaultive conduct), decided well before 2017, and sets out the governing tests (control, embeddedness, whose duty it was to prevent the act). The three highlights are all apt: para 81 confirms faultless vicarious liability and the deemed-employer finding; para 80 sets out the key indicia of deemed employment (uniform, integration, answering to Luminar management); para 28 states the central test for allocating responsibility.

ewca/civ/2008/173.rationale: The question concerns liability of an animal keeper (a zoo) for damage caused by an escaped animal (a penguin damaging a car). McKenny v Foster is squarely in the same doctrinal area: keeper's liability for damage caused by an escaped farm animal, applying the Animals Act 1971. It sets out the s.2(2) strict-liability framework (dangerous species limb rejected; the characteristics/knowledge/causation limb), stresses the causative-link requirement drawn from Mirvahedy and Curtis v Best, and addresses the foreseeability analysis in negligence and the effect of s.8 abolishing common-law restrictions on liability for straying animals. That is substantive and useful framework for a lawyer researching the penguin scenario, but it is not directly on point: no zoo, no dangerous/wild species, damage was a road accident to a car rather than property damage by a captive wild animal, and the outcome was that liability failed. Grade 2 rather than 3.
